parent.name: Pirc Defense
parent.overview: Black plays 1...d6 and, after 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3, ...g6 and ...Bg7, letting White build the broad e4-d4 centre and then undermining it from the flanks with ...c5 or ...e5 (hypermodern: the bigger White's centre, the bigger the target). The root is a crossroads: 1...d6 can transpose to the Philidor (3...e5 or ...c6) or to the Modern. White's replies run from sharp (Austrian Attack 4.f4, 150 Attack 4.Be3 with Qd2, Bh6 and h4-h5, Byrne 4.Bg5, Bayonet h4) to unhurried (Classical 4.Nf3 with Be2 and castling, fianchetto). Typical play is imbalanced: White gets space and often a kingside attack, Black gets a solid fianchettoed king and counterplay on the queenside and with central breaks. It is sound but has a reputation for giving White chances; Kasparov doubted it for the top level (s1), though Caruana, Anand and Grischuk have used it (s2).

parent.name: Petrov's Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 2.Nf3 by counter-attacking e4 rather than defending e5. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 d5 6.Bd3 both sides have lost an e-pawn and the structure is symmetrical, with the e-file the main open line. Black's aim is to equalise by quick development and piece trades; White tries to turn a small lead in development or slightly freer play into pressure, often castling and using the e-file or a queenside castling and pawn storm. The 3.d4 Steinitz line (3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.Nxe5 Nd7) and 3.Nc3 (Four Knights transposition) or 3.d3 sidelines give quieter or more varied structures. The main lines are widely played at the top and are known as drawish, though some lines hold real attacking chances for both sides.

parent.name: Van Geet Opening
parent.overview: White develops a knight to c3, controlling e4 and d5, and keeps the pawn structure undecided to choose a set-up once Black replies. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so Queen's Gambit and English structures are not available without reorganising. Main replies: 1...d5 (the cleanest; 2.e4 transposes to obscure Scandinavian lines, or the Van Geet Attack after 2...d4 3.Nce2), 1...e5 (then 2.e4 Vienna Game, the most common transposition in the database, or 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 Napoleon Attack), 1...Nf6 (one of the most unpleasant replies for White) and 1...c5 (transposing to Closed Sicilian or inferior-placed-knight lines). Sources call it sound and low-theory but unambitious: Black equalises with accurate play, so it earns points from surprise rather than from an edge, and masters play it under 1% of the time, though some strong correspondence players use it. The database root has few games itself; most of the subtree (about 290M games) is Vienna, Closed Sicilian and Chigorin-style transpositions that play like those openings.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: Smith-Morra Gambit
parent.overview: White offers a pawn on move 2 (2.d4 cxd4 3.c3) to swap the d-pawn for Black's c-pawn, gain a lead in development and open the c- and d-files. After 3...dxc3 4.Nxc3 White plays Nf3, Bc4 and quick castling, aiming at f7 with the Bc4, a Qe2/Rd1/Rc1 battery and tactical shots such as Nd5 and e5. Black either accepts and consolidates (typically with ...Nc6, ...e6, ...a6, ...Nge7-g6 or a Scheveningen/Kan set-up, trading pieces to hold the pawn) or declines with 3...Nf6, reaching a safe Alapin Sicilian. Play is open and tactical with White chasing the initiative; if Black consolidates the extra pawn he has good endgame chances.

parent.name: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation
parent.overview: This root is the King's Indian reached by the move order 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.c4 (the same position as 3.Nf3 in the 2.c4 move order). It is not a distinct opening: it is the ordinary King's Indian, where Black fianchettoes with ...Bg7, castles, and strikes at White's centre with ...e5, ...c5 or ...f5. White's choice of set-up decides the character: the classical 4.Nc3 and e4 leads to the locked-centre opposite-wing race (c4-c5 against ...f5-f4), while the Fianchetto Variation (g3, Bg2, O-O, Nc3) is quieter, positional, and has less forcing theory. The data subtree groups 4.e4 Normal Variation lines (the majority of games) under this root, so it mixes both. Black's success depends on timing and coordination rather than automatic aggression.

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation
parent.overview: After 3.e5 White gains space and fixes the centre; Black normally develops the light-squared bishop outside the chain with 3...Bf5 and then undermines the e5/d4 chain with ...c5 (often after ...e6), at times ...f6. White's set-ups range from the quiet Short System (Nf3, Be2, O-O, Be3 against ...c5) to aggressive kingside expansion with h4, g4 (Tal 4.h4, Bayonet 4.g4, Van der Wiel 4.Nc3 e6 5.g4, 4.Nf3 e6 5.Be2) aiming at a space and attack advantage. Typical positions are closed or semi-closed and French-like, with Black's bishop developed. It is the most popular way to fight the Caro-Kann in the 21st century and is double-edged: a space edge for White against a sound structure for Black.
